Return of the Webslinger BY JOE FORDHAM K emakes, reboots and 're-imaginings' have become standard Hollywood fare, but even the most battle-wearied movie industry speculators were surprised when Columbia Pictures and Marvel announced, in January 2010, that they were resetting the clock on their phenomenally popular Spider-Man motion picture series just three years after the completion of director Sam Raimi's original trilogy. Trade papers reported that The Amazing Spider-Man - with an all-new cast and villain - would be directed by Marc Webb, a filmmaker with mainly music videos, commercials and one romantic comedy to his name. "The spin was interesting," said senior visual effects supervisor Jerome Chen, a newcomer to the Spider-Man series, despite his long tenure at Sony Pictures Imageworks - the primary visual effects vendor for Raimi's trilogy. Marc had great respect for Sam Raimi and, in fact, he even consulted early on with Sam and some members of his team. But he was adamant that this was going to be a new vision, and he went so far as to say that he intended not to use anyone who had worked on any of the earlier Spider-Man films." 1 / 30 A number of Spidey veterans - including Imageworks - ultimately collaborated on

SPIDER-MAN Webb's film, which revisited Stan Lee's and Steve Ditko's origin story about Peter Parker (Andrew Garfield), a meek New York City science student who is transformed, via radioactive spider bite, into a web-shooting vigilante. The new adaptation - by James Vanderbilt, Alvin Sargent and Steve Kloves - interwove elements of Peter's personal history, including his abandonment by his parents, an event that leads him to seek out an old colleague of his father's, Dr. Curtis Connors (Rhys Ifans), a disabled, but brilliant genetic scientist at Oscorp Industries, whose failed attempt to regenerate his amputated arm transforms him into the Lizard, a nine-foot reptilian monster fixated on infecting the city's population with a similar mutation. The narrative also introduced Gwen Stacey (Emma Stone), a bright young classmate of Peter's and an intern at Oscorp, whom Peter confides in as his 'spider strength' develops. Peter's own genetic aberration, coupled with his affection for Gwen and his guilt by association with the deranged scientist, leads to a showdown atop the Oscorp tower. Returning to the team were production designer J. Michael Riva, a veteran of SpiderMan 3, and special effects supervisor John Frazier, a franchise regular, who collaborated with stunt coordinator Andy Armstrong to develop practical and mechanical effects. New team members included cinematographer John Schwartzman, who photographed the stereo 3D film using pairs of RED Epic digital cameras, in conjunction with 3Ality TS-5 stereography rigs. Jerome Chen led the visual effects initiative with visual effects producers Cari Thomas and John Clinton at Imageworks, the primary vendor. Other effects contributors included Legacy Effects, Pixomondo, Blur Studio, Pixel Playground, Nerve Studios 2 / 30 and half a dozen other vendors who generated additional effects and composites.

The mantra for all was an acute realism that would root Peter Parker's story in his SPIDER-MAN New York City home. "Marc had in mind a very raw image of the city," noted Chen. "The first conceptual mockups he showed me were of sets on the newly rebuilt Universal backlot, which had a 13-block replica of New York City. The art department had taken photos and done drawings on top, and it looked like everything was under construction, with scaffolding everywhere. I asked Michael Riva, 'What will it look like when you've finished building it?' Marc interjected, 'No, this is the look.' It was not the New York of Sam Raimi's movies, which was like a 1960s time capsule, very clean and pristine. This was more like how New York is today, with construction everywhere, and girders and skeletons of buildings covered with netting." he production, which would be based primarily in Los Angeles, shot establishing scenes with principat petarmers during a two weck shod in hew York Cit. Tran augment the location work, Imageworks CG supervisor John Haley and visual effects reference photographer Christopher Hebert gathered scenic images that included approximately 34,000 still images, aerial shots of SoHo and Chinatown, and tiled plates shot from rooftops at heights ranging from four to 80 stories above street level. We shot angle-specific plates and tiled plates for digital reconstructions of the environmenti explained Chen. iWe also did image acquisitions from very high vantage points as backgrounds for an end sequence on top of the Oscorp building, which needed a very extensive tiled environment.i 3 / 30 Imageworks used the scenic material to enhance its already considerable library of

SPIDER-MAN digital buildings, and generated 84 new buildings for layouts of up to 400 Manhattan high-rises. Adding to the complexity of the environment build, the majority of city scenes took place at night, which revealed interior details. "What primarily represents buildings at night are their illuminated windows," noted Chen. "It took a significant upgrade of our technology to render the color temperature of those interiors, with flickering televisions and light sources shining from inside. We also had to cater to the fact that our existing building models had been generated in RenderMan, whereas we now use Arnold, which is a completely different physics-based rendereri Imageworks captured imagery for window interiors using Visual Technologies' Spheron capture system, which yielded 360-degree 3D geometry and high dynamic range outputs of offices in New York and at Imageworks.iIf you look carefully, you might find John Haley's office or mine in a few shots, remarked Imageworks digital effects supervisor David Smith. "We used procedural propagation to place those in our building models, and our katana lighting system gave us the flexibility to make adjustments and then carry them from shot to shot. Our Arnold renderer allowed us to create levels of light reflection that increased depth and dimensionality, and it gave us the ability to use field geometry to create more accurate light responses and shadows. We got a lot closer to the buildings than we ever had before, so we had to upgrade those details.i Environment artists enhanced photographic reference with matte paintings to create sky domes, and used procedural simulations for atmospheric details and street traffic. "New York City has distinctive traffic patterns that are hard to build procedurally," noted 4 / 30 Smith. ¿We often animated vehicles by hand, and then we propagated those from block

SPIDER-MAN to block. For pedestrians, we mostly used Massive crowd simulations, but we also added a lot of details of people getting in and out of cabs, and other little textural elements. High-definition production plates placed demands on clarity of detail in city lighting. "It's the first time we've used the RED Epic camera," said Jerome Chen. "The dynamic range of the way it exposes night photography is very distinct. John Haley and I studied that endlessly to make sure our digital city at night felt like the plate photography. Window lights bloomed and revealed internal detail; some buildings had a green tint, others were more yellow, and others appeared blue. And street lighting really varied: sodium vapor street lamps had orange fill; storefronts appeared purple; one intersection might have warmer colors while others in the distance had cooler tones. It was a beautiful mix of colors, and we made sure we captured that quality in our CG streets. Imageworks' stereo imaging pipeline also had to be retooled to incorporate new levels of image fidelity. "We captured pairs of images at 5120x2560 pixels," said 3D visual effects supervisor Rob Engle, who shared duties on set with first-unit stereographer Eric Deren and second-unit stereographer Jason Goodman. "We framed ten percent smaller than the full image, and then went through a process of converting the images to 2276x1138 pixels, a resolution that worked well for digital effects. When we stripped away the ten-percent 'pad' from the image, that gave us a 2K picture that went out to theaters, and when that showed up in IMAX format, it was just spectacular. The compact nature of RED cameras and 3Ality rigs allowed relatively unrestricted camera motion, including wire-flown and handheld 3D shots. iWe shot a small part of the film in 2D, and 5 / 30 then converted, if we needed to get the camera into a tight space, or for specific effects

considerations. The majority of the film we captured native stereo. While digital environments underwent revamping, Spider-Man himself also received a makeover, guided by producers Avi Arad and Laura Ziskin, costume designer Kym Barrett and a team of concept artists. "We worked with the costume designer to distinguish the suit from previous films," explained conceptual designer Aaron Sims. "They wanted Spider-Man to appear younger, so we came up with interesting shapes for his silhouette, making his head bigger, and making him look lean and youthful, but still strong. We worked with 3D models, which allowed us to play around with sizes, angles, proportions, colors and textures." darker when it wasn't directly reflecting light," observed David Smith. "We put a huge amount of detail into layering textures, keeping in mind the image was going to be stereoscopic. The layers of different materials gave Spider-Man's suit a textural feel and a richness of detaili Though the filmmakers would have to use the digital Spider-Man in more extreme action sequences, they attempted to emphasize the physicality of Spider-Man's performance by using stunts and practical wire-flown effects as much as possible. 'Andy Armstrong had many early discussions analyzing how to really make a man swing from rope to rope," said Jerome Chen. "There had been stunts like that in the other movies, but SPIDER-MAN o build the digital Spider-Man, CG supervisor Chris Wagner referred to extensive photo reference of the practical suit in various lighting conditions. ¿The suit was textured with a honeycomb pattern that was sometimes reflective, but looked 6 / 30

SPIDER-MAN there's something very different in the rhythm of the way Spidey moves this time. An action sequence filmed on location in New York - in which Spider-Man pursues a criminal using a series of webs strung beneath the Riverside Drive Viaduct in West Harlem - set the tone for Spidey swings. ®They had a very elaborate stunt rig underneath a real bridge. They built a long track and had a stuntman, Ilram Choi, really swinging under the bridge, making very quick turns as he swung from web to web. They also had a drivable stunt rig supporting a huge truss, with Ilram on a pendulum-like device. That set the rhythm for how our virtual Spider-Man moved. Animation supervisor Randall William Cook oversaw character animation, working with a team of 43 animators and additional animation supervisor David Schaub, who joined the team partway through production as the workload increased.iOur methodology was to make the animation entertainingly real," said Cook. "There was a lot of stunt work; and by the time we got to the animation, we found that we were basing the style of Spider-Man's motion on Andrew Garfield's pantomime. In fact, Andrew had a guiding hand in all of Spider-Man's movement - in his own performance and in discussions with the stunt people. The stunt people attempted to evoke Andrew's interpretation of the Spider-Man comic book drawings. There was a unity of purpose there, and that affected our approach to visual effects. We concerned ourselves with the more death-defying moments that weren't possible in stunts, such as Spidey flying toward camera, missing it by feet, 20 stories over the main avenue below. That's not something you're going to attempt as a stunt in the real world." 7 1 30 Spider-Man animation took shape under the guidance of supervising animator Mike

SPIDER-MAN Beaulieu, who brought with him a passion for the source material.iMike has been a fan of the Spider-Man comics for a good long while," commented Cook. "He happily immersed himself in the character, and was very involved in keeping true to those referencesi While cognizant of classic Spidey poses, Cook urged animators to express the character beyond comic frames. 'You don't really have 'poses' in movies. If you look for a discrete frame to capture the essence of a scene, you won't find it: a smile might land on frame 87, the body posture might land on frame 92, and a hand gesture will land on frame 94. If you analyze really great animation, those emphases aren't real at all. In films like Ratatouille or Tangled - which have some of the best acting in animated characters I've seen - character models break from reality all the time. We stressed the hell out of our models to make them look good." o design Spider-Man's antagonist, the Lizard, the production explored creature concepts that expande or the comic glant bipedal epine. The actor party ing the Lizard had not been cast when we began conceptsi said Aaron Sims. "We began with a generic human appearance while we worked on ideas with Avi Arad. Then, when Marc Webb came on board, we incorporated design aspects that he liked from other concept artists the studio had employed. It was a very collaborative processi The design focused on humanizing Connors' reptilian alter ego. "We found that if we gave the Lizard a big crocodile head, as in the comic, we lost the humanity of the character; and so, we ended up discarding his big snouti 8 / 30 José Fernandez's Ironhead Studio sculpted clay renditions of the Lizard, which

SPIDER-MAN Legacy Effects used to generate 3D maquettes based on further conceptual work by lan Joyner, Scott Patton and Simon Webber. José's sculpture gave us the basic form of the Lizard," commented Lindsay Macgowan, who oversaw Legacy creature designs and makeup effects with Shane Mahan.i Our job was to detail that up and add a bit more of Rhys Ifans' likeness into the character. They already had the look of the proportions of the face. We did multiple versions with different texture patterns, and ended up with seven busts full-scale to Lizard's nine-foot height, with different colors, and eyes that ran the gamut from monstrous reptilian to human. lan Joyner detailed the final sculpture in Pixologic ZBrush, and then refined outputs milled from the 3D model. To get the amount of detail we needed, our model ended up being millions of polygons. We broke that into sections, and then created rapid prototype outputs. That created some 'jitter' in the scales, so we cleaned that up by sculpting by hand." Legacy supplied the production with a half-scale Lizard maquette and full-size busts in fiberglass and silicone. Marc Webb didn't want to use full-size animatronics on the shoot because he didn't know what the action was going to be," explained Shane Mahan. "We absolutely could have made an articulated bust that big; but having decided we were not going that route, we created reference as close to what the living creature would be so the visual effects team could capture images of the Lizard in the correct lighting. When we poured our silicone maquette, we made sure the material had a realistic translucency, and we did a paint job with washes of colors, then inserted painted resin teeth and glass eyes that reacted to light." 9 1 30 John Schwartzman and second-unit director of photography Peter Collister used

Legacy's maquettes to light scenes featuring the Lizard, while Jerome Chen's team captured high dynamic range images and clean background plates. Marc Webb then referred to animatics, which previsualization supervisor Gavin Wright generated at Proof, to guide creature blocking. iMarc referred to District 9 as an example of how he wanted CG to be integrated," remarked Jerome Chen. "It wasn't so much the process they had used on that film that he was interested in; it was more about the organic feel of how the shots fit together. He didn't want creature scenes to appear staged as big effects moments; he wanted them to be incidental to the story." 'We created silicone and Pros-Aide appliances for his face, neck and back, in three difterent stages. Richie Alonzo sculpted the majority of those pieces with Mark Maitre and Akihito Ikeda; and then Richie applied those with makeup department head Ve Neill. Shane and I accompanied the shoot whenever Rhys was in makeup. on set wearing padding that expanded his six-foot-nine frame to Lizard proportions. "Jason wore a periscope attachment on top of his head for eye-lines," said Randy Cook. ¿Depending upon his carriage, that brought his eye-line up to about seven and a half feet, so his full height would have been about nine feet talli Imageworks extrapolated from on-set interactions with keyframe animation.iThe Lizard needed strength that was SPIDER-MAN cenes of Connors transforming back and forth into the Lizard employed combinations of prosthetics and digital effects.iWe generated quite a few makeups for Rhys Ifans going into and out of his transformations, said Lindsay Macgowan. To shoot full Lizard scenes, creature performer Jason Barnes portrayed the Lizard 10 / 30

SPIDER-MAN appropriate to his mass. If you're standing next to a horse and the horse happens to look over, he can knock you on your ass because he doesn't know his own strength. We tried to bring that to the Lizard. We didn't want him to do anything that was wildly impossible. We wanted to make him stronger than the fittest stuntman, and so we'd often change Jason's pantomime." CG supervisor Theo Bialek oversaw creation of digital Lizard models, working from Legacy's maquette and nature reference. We looked at chameleons, iguanas, desertbased lizards and komodo dragons," recalled Jerome Chen. "We had a team of artists who worked in ZBrush and became very familiar with lizard scale patterns, the width between scales and the way dirt accumulates between them. Those were not procedurally generated. We hand-painted all the scales in very beautiful texture maps. The final creature, generated in Mudbox, resulted in a 128-million polygon construction, one of the largest character models in Imageworks' history. Creature artists then rigged rotations and translations of limbs and joints, muscle animation and dynamic simulations. "We rigged automatic effects like flesh and skin jiggle," said David Smith. "But procedural responses didn't take into account independent muscle movement, so we gave the animators controls to create moments when the Lizard flexed and tensed his muscles. The Lizard's skin slid and bunched using a form of cloth simulation. We had standardized settings, but then we had another layer of control that we could adjust by hand. That was especially important around the Lizard's neck where the skin was loose and leathery, like a komodo. That created very interesting responses and helped accen11 / 30 tuate his scale as his skin folded and wrinkled.

SPIDER-MAN Lizard facial animation included multi-layered eyes detailed for full-screen closeups. 'The eyeballs contained 3D geometry that allowed us to change the shape of his pupil from round to a reptile slit," said Smith. "We created a sense of depth in his iris using geometry and displacements, and we added rigging that allowed the eyes to drift. The eye is made up of very soft tissue, which allows the pupil to move from side to side if you shake your head around. We built that into our model, so if the Lizard moved his head abruptly, the pupil would drift behind. That level of detail, combined with the physical accuracy of the lighting hitting the iris and refracting, created a rich sense of depthii For Peter's initial encounter with Dr. Connors, Marc Webb filmed characters entering the Oscorp building at Hearst Tower in midtown Manhattan. Michael Riva and conceptual designer George Hull then developed the building as a soaring structure of glass and steel, which Imageworks created as a digital construct rising above lower floors built of more classical stonework. onnors greets his visitors in an upper-level laboratory, the stump of his ampua soundstage set, with Rhys Ifans wearing a greenscreen sleeve over his right arm. Pixomondo digitally removed Connors' arm in 70 shots, in a variety of scenes and lighting scenarios. "Marc did not want Connors' amputated arm to be something that was difficult to look at," said Pixomondo visual effects supervisor Boris Schmidt. "It's an old wound that has healed, and Connors has very much integrated it into his persona. 12 / 30 It had to appear authentic, where details in the scarring were clearly visible, but we didn't

want it to scream for attention." SPIDER-MAN Placement of the amputation sever-point, located just above Connors' right elbow, varied according to his wardrobe. They took a little bit of artistic license with the cut point," commented Pixomondo CG supervisor Adam Watkins. "On set, Rhys rarely had any tracking markers on the green sock on his arm, so we matchmoved his whole upper torso to get correct position and placement of the stump. We had to replace any shadowing from Rhys' real arm, and in many shots we completely replaced the bottom half of Connor's lab coat because the coat often flapped around his green arm as he walked around." To generate the nub, Pixomondo researched images of amputees and devised a 3D model with realistic fleshy detail.iOur longest shot was of Connors looking in a mirror in his undershirt, with the camera relatively close to the stump. To blend our CG arm into his exposed shoulder, we had to be very precise with subsurface scattering and the colors of the shadowingi Adding to the challenge of digitally rebuilding plates featuring Connors' amputated limb, Ifans sometimes wore an arm brace to restrict his range of movement. In some of the raw plates, Rhys held a small stick on the inside of his hand within the greenscreen sock," said Pixomondo visual effects producer Natasha Ozoux. "The stick went halfway up the inside of his bicep into his shirt, preventing Rhys from bending his arm at the elbow, and helping restrict his shoulder motion. That meant we had a bigger volume to remove and repaint. But Rhys did a terrific job in maintaining the composure of a real amputee." 13 / 30 Connors activates a holographic display in his laboratory to instruct visiting students

SPIDER-MAN in his trans-species gene splicing techniques. Later, he uses the hologram as a scientific interface, working with Peter in experiments to develop mutagenic serum. Webb filmed scenes of the hologram, known as the 'Tree of Life,' using interactive lighting effects on set. Blur Studio then generated interactive stereographic animation. We based the hologram design on a double helix," said Blur Studio creative director Tim Miller. "It was an instantly recognizable graphical representation of this virtual laboratory where Connors could try out DNA sequencing mixes from different types of animals. He focuses on reptiles for their ability to regrow lost limbs, but also samples genetic material from elsewhere in the animal kingdom." The tour-group hologram featured rectilinear lines connecting branches representing different genus. "We had humans, rats, spiders, wasps and all these other animals forming the Tree of Life," related CG lead artist Colin James. "For the later scene, we created a mutated mouse, called Freddy, on which Connors tries to regrow a missing limb using lizard DNA. We modeled freddy and the lizard in ZBrush, using a morph target to animate mutations, and rendered the creatures with an x-ray holographic look. We gave them animated skeletal structures and veins, then we rendered a fog pass and a fresnel pass." Blur Studio layered elements in Eyeon Digital Fusion, placing them in stereo space within a cylinder of blue light, and aligned motion graphics to interactions of Andrew Garfield's fingers as he mimed operation of virtual keyboard controls. While first visiting Oscorp, Peter gains entry to a classified chamber where he discovers a horde of spiders engaged in the production of biocable, a synthetic fiber with 14 / 30 a tensile strength hundreds of times stronger than steel. Imageworks effects animation

lead Joseph Pepper oversaw biocable creation using digital simulations rendered with a distinctive hue that foreshadowed Spider-Man livery. We played on the idea that the spiders' silk was genetically engineered to give off a slightly refractive qualityi noted Jerome Chen, "cuing in red and blue colors as it refracts." Inside the web production chamber, Michael Riva's team designed high-tech machinery upon which spiders scuttled. Imageworks digitally generated mechanical looms and animated tiny spiders, one of which bites Peter on the neck.iWe keyframed machinery turning and sliding back and forth, drawing web into the machine explained Randy Cook.iWe then generated a library of spider animation that CG supervisor Robert Winter replicated in Massive crowd simulations. He placed those on the webs and keyframed spiders dropping onto Peter." Back home, Peter discovers a painful wound in the back of his neck, with a spider still attached. The production filmed the scene with Andrew Garfield manipulating a small metal weight on a monofilament. Imageworks then replaced the prop with a CG web and spider corpse. ground only removing safety wires in post. Wirework and stunt rigging were also used for subsequent scenes of Peter acclimatizing to his new powers during an altercation with a gang of back-alley muggers whom he outruns in a dazzling display of parkour-like leaps and bounds. Pixel Playground supplied rig removals and made sparing use of a digital SPIDER-MAN he spider bite imbues Peter with athletic abilities that manifest as he practices on his skateboard and hurtles his body around a warehouse full of dangling chains - acrobatics that were achieved solely with stunt work, with Pixel Play15 1 30

SPIDER-MAN double as Peter vaults a wide gap between buildings. Peter takes inspiration from his newfound abilities to build homemade mechanical spinnerets, adapting cartridges of Oscorp biocable into wristwatch-like dispensers that project tendrils of sticky fiber. "All the webs in the film are CG," commented Jerome Chen. "We took the elasticity of real spider webs as reference, and animated them to coil in an accordion pattern. As they stretch out, webs become more taut, with layers of coils around each filament. The center core was very straight, and then multiple strands wrapped around that like DNA coils, with little barbs coming off to catch the light. We rendered the webs to be translucent, not completely refractive like glass, and it took many months before we determined the look. Animators described web trajectories using spline curves, which Joseph Pepper's effects team then used to guide simulations.iWe generated the web core and wrapped geometry around that," related David Smith. "We could manipulate those in size and detail; and, for super closeups, we did custom builds of webs that had their own levels of depth and dimensionality ray-traced in fine detail. In fact, we rendered all web elements at 4K in order to ray-trace the refractive and reflective qualities, so, as simple as they are - essentially a line - webs were fairly expensive to render, but that gave them a special quality." Peter first puts bio-cable through its paces while attempting a rooftop handstand from which he tumbles and then swings between high-rise buildings. Garfield performed the handstand on a bluescreen set, supported by wire rigging. Imageworks added a 16 / 30 vertiginous down-view of the street and animated a takeover to a digital Spidey as the

camera jibbed over Peter's feet and generated the fall with keyframe animation. To convey the terror and exhilaration of plunging and swinging on webs, Imageworks animated point-of-view shots, allowing the audience to see through Peter's eyes. 'We tried to create camera moves that a cinematographer might use to depict a subjective point of view, noted Randy Cook. "It wasn't literally 'helmet cam' style footage. That would have had a very different look, out of keeping with the film, but we wanted to evoke Peter's experience as a roof-leaping Spider-Man." Spidey POVs required judicious use of stereographic effects to maintain illusions of depth. "There's a limited amount of parallax that can effectively convey a stereo image," said Rob Engle. "It is known as the 'depth budget,' and we had to figure out how to maximize the use of that. In some POV shots, stereo space was taken up entirely by a foreground object if Spider-Man's leg or arm reached into view. Other times, we focused on creating depth in the 'negative space' between foreground and background. And we never wanted Spider-Man to get too close to the background, unless he was literally meant to touch it. appliance, which Rhys Ifans wore while seated at a workbench.iMarc wanted to see an embryonic arm that looked like an unborn baby's tissue," said Shane Mahan. "We painted Rhys' arm and hand garishly white and veiny. Over that, he slipped on a translucent veiny SPIDER-MAN onnors meanwhile begins his own transformation after injecting himself as the first human test subject of his mutagenic serum, causing his amputated arm to regrow. Legacy Effects created Connors' arm regeneration using a prosthetic 17 / 30

SPIDER-MAN silicone prosthetic. We blended that down and applied layers of skin-like materials that Rhys used his left hand to pull apart, revealing his new arm beneath. We prefabricated the layers. The exterior was harder and more translucent, created by layering silicone into a mold with different colored slime, pieces of thread and yarn. We created interior portions out of softer layers of cellulose paper and gluei Pixomondo then generated digital effects of Connors' regenerated tissue giving way to more dominant reptile DNA. iWe grew a lizard claw, skin and scales that burst out of the gelatinous mass covering his hand," said Natasha Ozoux. "Imageworks shared its Lizard model with us, and we modified the size of the claw to make it fit to the prosthetic." Connors covers his claw and hurries to show his breakthrough to Oscorp executive Rajit Ratha (Irfan Khan), who has departed the building in a limousine. Pixomondo continued Connors' transformation, enhancing prosthetics in shots of Ifans seated inside a taxicab, and animated Lizard scales spreading across the character's arm and head. The transformation culminates in Connors ripping through the taxi roof and continuing on foot, fully transformed into the Lizard, seeking Ratha's limousine in gridlock traffic on the Williamsburg Bridge. The production shot establishing scenes around the bridge location, and then built a 100-foot section of the structure backed by bluescreen above Falls Lake at Universal Studios. A Farewell to Arms BY JODY DUNCAN C hristopher Nolan may be the only current A-list film director who would make a large-scale, big-budget superhero movie with fantastical flying machines, multiple dynamic chase sequences, and spectacular, cataclysmic events - and rack up a total of only 450 visual effects shots. It was especially noteworthy given that the film was the final entry in Nolan's lauded 'Dark Knight Trilogy,' which quite reasonably raised audience expectations for action and spectacle - expectations that Nolan more than met in The Dark Knight Rises, a film that combines all the classic elements of the disaster and war movie genres. Rather than populating chaotic street scenes with Massive-simulated crowds, Nolan and his producers went to great pains to hire, costume, wrangle and shoot thousands of extras on locations in Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and New York. Rather than relying on a computer generated flying 'Bat' - Batman's newest mode of transportation - the Nolan team shot a practical Bat, mounting it to the top of a truck and then racing it through city streets as cameras rolled. And rather than enjoying the freedom and relative ease of 1/36 generating digital aircraft for an audacious aerial sequence that opens the film, Nolan

DARK KNIGHT spent eight months coordinating with department heads and authorities in the U.h. to shoot aerialists executing breathtaking stunts on real planes in the skies over rural Scotland. Even the bold and in-camera-minded Nolan had to rely on visual effects for some shots, however. "Chris has a bit of a reputation for not really caring for visual effects," noted visual effects producer Mike Chambers, "but that isn't exactly true. For Chris, visual effects are just another tool to be used sparingly and wisely - but never as a crutch or an easy fix. The focus is always: 'Where do we need visual effects to tell the story in a way that I can't photograph myself? And if and when we do use visual effects, you'd better make sure they look like I photographed them!'" To deliver those crucial visual effects shots, Nolan turned to visual effects supervisor Paul Franklin and the creative team at Double Negative, the sole effects house on the show.iI had worked with Paul and the guys at Double Negative on the last couple of films," said Christopher Nolan, "and I wanted to get back to the more old-fashioned approach of working with one group of visual effects artists, rather than farming things out to five or six different companies around town. I wanted a visual effects team that would be very much a part of the production, developing things long before we started shooting. Paul Franklin was an integral part of the development of The Dark Knight Rises, and it was a great advantage to be working with somebody with whom I had such a great history." Despite the relatively modest shot count, Franklin and the crew at Double Negative 2/36 had their work cut out for them with The Dark Knight Rises. Many of the effects shots

were quite lengthy, and 350 of the 450 were done at full IMAX resolution. We were dealing with a much larger area of negative," said Paul Franklin, who worked alongside visual effects co-supervisors Peter Bebb and Andrew Lockley, and visual effects producer Claudia Dehmel at Double Negative to deliver the show,and that translated into very highresolution 8K scans. Render times became much longer, because we were rendering roughly eight times the screen area of a standard 2h image, and we had to have a lot more storage space. We allocated something like 250 terabytes of online storage to this show; and in the end, I think we used closer to 400 terabytes. It was a huge amount of data to wrangle. Fortunately, we'd dealt with that on The Dark Knight, so a lot of the infrastructure was already in place; but the amount of IMAX material was greatly increased on this show. We also did all of our regular 35mm work at 4K, which we've been doing for Chris' films since The Dark Knight. 'Old-school' was not the vision of director Len Wiseman when he embarked on recreating Total Recall 22 years later.
